Vignette:
Priya Sharma had come to believe that the night the Riverside Convention Center’s east annex collapsed was less a memory than a fever dream. It had begun on a Tuesday evening, just as she was clocking out from her third shift as an intensive care nurse. A compromised gas main had detonated, followed by a roar that turned the sub-basement into a suffocating canyon of dust and twisted rebar. She remembered the jarring impact of being thrown against a concrete pillar, the sharp snap of a seatbelt locking across her ribs, and the sudden, metallic groan of collapsing steel. When the dust finally settled, the scale of the destruction had left her certain that the event was too extreme to be real. The sheer impossibility of entire walls vanishing, the cinematic violence of it all, had made her question whether she had actually been there or if it was some distant news broadcast she had watched. Over the following weeks, Priya noticed her recollection refusing to settle. The event arrived in disconnected pieces that never aligned: a shard of glass catching a strobe light, the hollow echo of her own footsteps on broken tile, the sight of a discarded work badge half-buried in rubble, then suddenly she was staring at a fractured support beam. These fragments popped up without warning, each one isolated and impossible to sequence. She found herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it. When the pieces began to surface during quiet moments—while washing her hands, while waiting for an elevator, while listening to a phone ring—her mind would simply go blank, a sudden white wall erected between her and the past. She had come to believe that holding onto the pieces was impossible. By the time she returned to work at County General, the habits had already taken root. Priya found herself mapping her clinical rotations around the hospital’s east wing, a corridor that still carried the faint scent of burnt insulation and echoed with the periodic groan of aging ventilation pipes. When that groan sounded, or when a defibrillator beeped nearby, her chest would tighten and her pulse would spike. She began taking the service elevators to avoid the ground-floor waiting area, where the heavy thud of a dropped IV pole sounded too much like shifting debris. She avoided the hospital’s annual disaster drills, claiming chronic migraines instead of standing in a crowded assembly hall. The consequences accumulated steadily. She missed two trauma bay coverage shifts because she could not bring herself to walk past the loading dock. Her charge nurse noticed how Priya would abruptly step back when maintenance workers moved metal toolboxes near the supply room, how she left early on days when structural repairs echoed from the basement. What frightened Priya most was the erosion of her own steadiness. She was a nurse; she relied on precision, on the ability to hold space in a crisis. Lately, she had caught herself hesitating over medication orders when the monitor alarms chimed in rapid succession, certain that the noise would shatter her focus entirely. Priya walked into the clinic with a referral slip and a quiet, exhausted hope. She was tired of the white walls her mind erected, tired of circling the hospital’s east wing like a ghost in her own career. She wanted to remember without flinching. She wanted to trust that the ground beneath her was solid, and that the past, however extreme, had actually ended.
